name: Fukuda Chiyo-ni (Kaga no Chiyo)
credit: Utagawa Kuniyoshi, Kaga no Chiyo at the well, c. 1840 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Fukuda Chiyo-ni (1703–1775), often called Kaga no Chiyo, was a haikai poet of Kaga province, on the Japan Sea coast. One of the best-known women poets of the Edo period, she became a Buddhist nun in 1754, and is remembered above all for her morning-glory verse, in which a well-bucket entangled by the vines is left undisturbed.

These are the hokku that Basil Hall Chamberlain attributes to her in Bashō and the Japanese Poetical Epigram (1902), in romaji with his English renderings where he gives verse. For the morning-glory verse and two others he offers only a literal gloss or a prose paraphrase, which is not reproduced here.

poems.title: Hyaku-nari ya
poems.author: Fukuda Chiyo-ni (Kaga no Chiyo)
poems.text:
Hyaku-nari ya
Tsuru hito-suji no
Kokoro yori

poems.title: Hyaku-nari ya
poems.author: Fukuda Chiyo-ni (Kaga no Chiyo)
poems.text:
A hundred tendrils, yea! and all
From the same vine that is their heart.

poems.title: Hototogisu
poems.author: Fukuda Chiyo-ni (Kaga no Chiyo)
poems.text:
Hototogisu
Hototogisu tote
Ake ni keri

poems.title: Shibukaro ka
poems.author: Fukuda Chiyo-ni (Kaga no Chiyo)
poems.text:
Shibukaro ka
Shiranedo kaki no
Hatsu-chigiri

poems.title: Okite mitsu
poems.author: Fukuda Chiyo-ni (Kaga no Chiyo)
poems.text:
Okite mitsu
Nete mitsu kaya no
Hirosa kana

poems.title: Okite mitsu
poems.author: Fukuda Chiyo-ni (Kaga no Chiyo)
poems.text:
Whether I lay me down or wake,
How large seems the mosquito-net!

poems.title: Tombo-tori
poems.author: Fukuda Chiyo-ni (Kaga no Chiyo)
poems.text:
Tombo-tori
Kyō wa dokora ye
Itta yara

poems.title: Tombo-tori
poems.author: Fukuda Chiyo-ni (Kaga no Chiyo)
poems.text:
Where may he have gone off to-day,—
The hunter after dragon-flies?

poems.title: Hito-kakae
poems.author: Fukuda Chiyo-ni (Kaga no Chiyo)
poems.text:
Hito-kakae
Aredo yanagi wa
Yanagi kana

poems.title: Hito-kakae
poems.author: Fukuda Chiyo-ni (Kaga no Chiyo)
poems.text:
A willow may an armful be,
But ’tis a willow all the same.
